title: The line Jayadeva couldn't write
hookLine: a poet can't bring himself to write one line about God, goes to bathe, and comes back to find it written
carry: in bhakti, love runs both ways: sometimes God bows
tomorrow: jnana: Ramana Maharshi, and the afternoon he lay down to die
last: DHARMA BEGINS AT YOUR OWN DOOR.

lines: A LINE TOO BOLD TO WRITE.
cards: Eastern India, centuries ago. A poet named Jayadeva is writing a long Sanskrit poem about Krishna and Radha, the gopi Krishna loves.
He reaches a scene where Krishna, having hurt Radha, pleads with her to forgive him, and the line that comes to Jayadeva is shocking. Krishna asks Radha to place her foot on his head.
God, asking a cowherd girl to put her foot on him. Jayadeva can't write it. It feels like too much.
So he puts down his pen and goes to the river to bathe.

teach.h: THE GITA GOVINDA: SONG OF THE COWHERD.
teach.b: The poem is the Gita Govinda, the song of the cowherd, and the story people tell goes on. While Jayadeva is at the river, his wife, Padmavati, sees him come back, pick up the manuscript, write something, and leave again.

teach.h: THE LINE WRITTEN WHILE HE BATHED.
teach.b: Then Jayadeva walks in from the river, dripping, and finds the line already written: the one he couldn't bring himself to write. Who wrote it? You did, she says.
You came back a few minutes ago. And he understands, the story says, that Krishna himself came and finished the line. That's a legend, not history.
But look at what it's saying.

The poem tells of spring in the forest, Krishna wandering among the gopis, Radha hurt and jealous and hiding, a friend carrying messages between them, Krishna's longing and apology, and finally their reunion.
It reads like a love poem, and it is one. Devotees hear it as the soul and God: the soul's hurt, God's longing, and a love so real that God would bow to the one who loves him.
That's the heart of the line Jayadeva couldn't write, and a real teaching of bhakti: love runs both ways. The devotee longs for God, and God longs for the devotee. God isn't only the one we bow to.
These songs are still sung at the Jagannath temple in Puri. And they change how an apology looks. If even God, in this poem, asks to be forgiven, then bowing first isn't losing.

how: The Gita Govinda's songs are sung in temple worship, including at the Jagannath temple in Puri, and are performed in Odissi and other classical dance; devotees hear the love of Radha and Krishna as the love between the soul and God.

o: a stillness where nothing at all is done
a ritual duty to bow before the gods
action, even God's own act of bowing in love

s: in the legend, Jayadeva finished the line after his bath
he found it already written. his wife said he'd come back and written it; he understood it was Krishna.
the Gita Govinda is about Radha and Krishna
spring, jealousy, messages carried by a friend, longing and reunion.
the Gita Govinda is part of the Bhagavad Gita
it's a separate Sanskrit poem by Jayadeva. Govinda means the cowherd.

games.q: you're Jayadeva. the next line has Krishna asking Radha to put her foot on his head. it feels far too bold. what do you do?
o: put down the pen and go bathe.
games.why: he goes to the river. when he returns, the line is written. the story says Krishna came and wrote it himself.

practice: Think of a time someone you'd hurt forgave you, or a time you forgave someone, and stay with the moment the distance closed, without replaying the whole argument.

On the in-breath, feel what it's like to be taken back; on the out-breath, what it's like to take someone back: those two feelings are the whole poem. If you pray, you can rest in God's longing for you.

wordCard.voice: Karma, action, is the word these weeks carry. In the Gita Govinda, the boldest action belongs to God: bowing to the one he loves.

orig.note: Sanskrit: gita, song + govinda, the cowherd, a name of Krishna. Jayadeva's poem.
